title: {{NAME}} and the Herd That Crossed the Silver River
moral: When you share what makes you different, you give others permission to be themselves too.

pages.content:
The silver river had no name in any language that humans had written down, which was perhaps because it was not entirely made of water. It ran clear and cold and tasted of apple blossom in spring, but at night its surface threw back not the sky above but the sky of some other, deeper place, full of constellations that did not match any chart.

{{NAME}} had found it by following a white deer through a wood where the trees grew in spirals. The deer had vanished at the water's edge. {{NAME}} had not vanished. He had sat down on the bank and waited, because the deer had seemed purposeful and purposeful things, he had learned, generally arrived at something worth waiting for.

The unicorn herd came downstream at dusk: seven of them, their horns catching the last of the light and scattering it across the water in long ribbons of gold and rose. They were every colour that horses come in, and some they do not. The smallest was deep charcoal grey with a horn like twisted moonstone. She noticed {{NAME}} immediately and stopped, ankle-deep in the silver water, and looked at him with calm, direct, enormous violet eyes.

pages.content:
The charcoal unicorn waded closer. Her name, {{NAME}} would learn, was Silt, a name she had chosen herself because she liked the way it felt in her mouth, which said a great deal about her personality.

The other unicorns watched from a cautious distance, shifting their weight, their horns dipping and rising like the needles of compasses in an uncertain field. They were wary. All except one chestnut mare who had the patient, calculating look of a creature waiting to see what the cautious ones were so worried about.

{{NAME}} sat very still. Silt's nose reached his cheek and stopped a breath away. Her breath smelled of clover and cold water. Her violet eyes moved across his face the way someone reads a sentence they want to make sure they have understood correctly.

{{NAME}}'s face was soft with wonder, eyes wide, a smile spreading so slowly it seemed to happen against his will, pulled out of him by the simple impossible beauty of having a unicorn this close.

'Hello,' he said, very quietly, as though speaking at normal volume might break something important.

pages.content:
The problem, Silt explained, was the crossing. The silver river was low enough to ford in all the wide, gentle stretches except one: the bend around the black granite bluff, where the current ran fast and cold and deep, and where the herd needed to cross to reach their winter grazing on the far bank.

Normally they crossed at the bend in shallow season. This year the water was higher than usual. Six of the seven could swim it. Silt was the seventh. She was young, small, and for all her tremendous personality, not yet a strong swimmer. She had told no one in the herd this. The chestnut mare, whose name was Orla, had noticed anyway and had been waiting, with the patience of someone who understood pride, for Silt to ask.

{{NAME}} waded into the river beside Silt without needing it explained. The current at the bend pushed against them both like a living thing. He kept one hand gently in her mane. She kept her shoulder against his side. Orla swam on Silt's other flank. Together the three of them moved through the deepest channel, slow and unsteady, then steadier, then through.

pages.content:
On the far bank, Silt shook herself from nose to tail in a long, satisfying shudder that sent silver droplets in every direction, and {{NAME}} sat on the grass soaking wet and laughing.

Orla stood over them both, dripping, looking at {{NAME}} with an expression he recognised: it was the look of someone who has just revised their opinion of a person significantly upward. It was a good feeling to be on the receiving end of.

Then the herd gathered around Silt, not in the anxious circling of before, but in the particular way of animals who feel something has been set right. Silt stood in the centre of them, small and charcoal-grey and bright-eyed, and for the first time in the whole crossing she looked completely unguarded.

She turned her moonstone horn toward {{NAME}} and pressed it, very lightly, to his braided bracelet. A warmth moved up his arm and into his chest, quiet and golden as the last of the light. The bracelet threads, silver and gold, caught an extra gleam and held it.

pages.content:
The winter grazing meadow on the far bank was soft and wide and smelled of cold grass and possibility. The herd spread out across it with the comfortable ease of creatures arriving somewhere they had been looking forward to.

Silt settled beside {{NAME}} in the long grass at the meadow's edge. He leaned against her warm flank and looked up at the sky, which was deep indigo now and showing the strange, extra constellations that lived above the silver river. The ones that were not on any chart.

Orla grazed nearby, moving slowly and deliberately, watching nothing in particular with the deep content of someone who has done exactly what they set out to do.

{{NAME}}'s eyes were growing soft and warm. His bracelet still carried that faint extra gleam and his chest still held that quiet golden warmth. Silt's breathing was steady and slow and absolutely certain of itself, nothing like the hesitation at the river's edge.

Goodnight, silver-crossed traveller. Close your eyes, and wonder what constellation only you can see from where you are.
